n: The heavens and earth and all their “host”—everything in them—are completed.

f.g: All their multitude of inhabitants and elements.

n: On the seventh day God finished and rested from his work, seeing that it was good.

f.w: I rested on the seventh day

n: God blessed the seventh day and made it holy—the origin of the Sabbath.

f.g: Made it holy; set it apart.

n: This is the account (the “generations”) of how the heavens and earth were made.

f.g: History or account of origins (Hebrew toledot).

n: A distinctive Latter-day Saint teaching: God created all things spiritually before they existed physically on earth. All people were first created in heaven as spirits before there was flesh on earth.

f.w: before they were naturally upon the face of the earth
f.g: There was a spirit creation before the physical one.

n: A mist rose from the ground to water the land.
God formed man’s body from the earth and breathed life into him; he became a living soul—spirit and body united. Adam was the first flesh on the earth.

f.w: formed man from the dust of the ground

f.g: In Latter-day Saint scripture, the soul is spirit and body together.

f.w: the first flesh upon the earth
f.g: Interpreted variously; often understood as Adam being the first mortal.

n: God planted a garden eastward in Eden and placed the man there.
God made beautiful trees grow, which were also “living souls,” created spiritually first. In the garden’s center were the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.

f.w: the tree of knowledge of good and evil

n: A river flowed out of Eden and divided into four headwaters.
The first river, Pison, surrounded the land of Havilah, rich in gold.

f.g: Usually spelled Pishon; its location is unknown.

n: Havilah’s gold was good, and it also had bdellium and onyx.

f.g: Probably an aromatic resin, or possibly a precious stone; uncertain.

n: The second river, Gihon, surrounded the land of Ethiopia (Hebrew Cush).

f.g: Hebrew Cush; its exact identity in this passage is uncertain.

n: The third river, Hiddekel (the Tigris), flowed east of Assyria; the fourth was the Euphrates. These names were familiar to Israel and anchor Eden in the known world.

f.g: The Hebrew name for the Tigris River.

n: God placed Adam in the garden to tend and care for it. Work was part of Eden from the start.

f.w: to dress it, and to keep it
f.g: Dress = cultivate; keep = guard or care for.

n: Adam may freely eat from every tree.
A crucial addition to Genesis: Adam is forbidden the tree of knowledge, yet “thou mayest choose for thyself.” God gives both a command and agency, and warns of death.

f.w: thou mayest choose for thyself, for it is given unto thee

n: God tells his Only Begotten it’s not good for man to be alone, so he will make “an help meet” for him—a fitting companion.

f.g: Two words: a “help” that is “meet” (suitable, corresponding). Hebrew ‘ezer kenegdo—a partner equal to and suited for him; ‘ezer is used of God himself.

n: God brings the animals to Adam to name. They too are living souls, given the breath of life.

f.w: whatsoever Adam called every living creature

n: Adam names all the animals, but none is a suitable partner for him.

f.w: there was not found an help meet for him

n: God causes a deep sleep to fall on Adam and takes one of his ribs. Many Latter-day Saint leaders have described the rib account as figurative.

f.g: Often understood symbolically: woman is created from man’s side, as his equal partner.

n: From the rib God makes the woman and brings her to Adam.
Adam rejoices: “bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.” She is called Woman because she came from man—a wordplay in Hebrew (ishshah/ish).

f.w: bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh

n: This is the foundation of marriage: a man leaves his parents and cleaves to his wife, and they become one. Jesus quoted this verse.
They were naked and not ashamed—innocent, with no self-consciousness before the Fall.
